title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) Pattern
oneLiner: Separates the write path (commands) from the read path (queries), letting each be modeled and scaled independently.

hero.name: The Splitter
hero.catchphrase: Reading and writing are different jobs. Stop making one model do both.
hero.power: Splits commands (validated, transactional writes) from queries (fast, denormalized reads), letting each be optimized entirely on its own terms.
hero.weakness: Introduces real complexity — most notably eventual consistency between the write and read models — that's only worth paying when read and write patterns genuinely diverge at scale.
hero.origin: The Splitter appeared after a single Order model tried to serve both a heavily-validated checkout write path and a dashboard needing fast, denormalized reads across millions of orders — one model, two incompatible jobs.

story.problem: The Order model handles both checkout (heavily validated, transactional writes) and the analytics dashboard (fast reads across millions of denormalized order records). Optimizing one path keeps breaking the other.
story.solution: The Splitter separates the two entirely. Commands (`PlaceOrder`) go through a validated, transactional write model. Queries (`GetOrderSummary`) read from a separate, denormalized read model optimized purely for fast lookups.
story.result: The write model stays strict and transactional, focused only on correctness. The read model is denormalized and indexed purely for speed — each optimized for its own actual job.

before: One model serves both validated writes and fast reads
Optimizing reads risks weakening write correctness, and vice versa
Read and write scaling needs are forced to match each other
after: Commands and queries use separate, independently optimized models
The write model stays strict; the read model stays fast
Read and write paths scale independently, matching their actual load

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A dashboard query joins six tables and takes 8 seconds, while the same Order model also handles strict checkout validation.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Every time I denormalize for dashboard speed, I risk breaking the strict validation checkout depends on. One model can't do both well.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Splitter appears holding two distinct tools — one precise, one broad — for two very different jobs.
panels.speaker: The Splitter
panels.dialogue: Stop forcing one model to write correctly AND read fast. Split them. Commands go one way, queries go another.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: PlaceOrderCommand writes through a strict, transactional write model. GetOrderSummaryQuery reads from a separate, denormalized read model.
panels.speaker: The Splitter
panels.dialogue: The write model only cares about correctness. The read model only cares about speed. Neither compromises for the other anymore.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The dashboard query drops from 8 seconds to 40 milliseconds, with checkout validation untouched.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Dashboard queries are 200x faster, and checkout validation didn't change at all. Both finally get what they actually need.

useWhen: Read and write workloads have genuinely different performance, consistency, or scaling requirements.
A single model has become a bottleneck trying to serve both strict transactional writes and fast, flexible reads.
You're already using event-driven architecture, making it natural to keep a read model in sync via events.
avoidWhen: Read and write patterns are similar enough that one model serves both perfectly well.
The team can't yet handle the operational complexity of eventual consistency between write and read models.
The application's scale doesn't actually justify the added architectural complexity — CQRS is a scaling pattern, not a default.
commonMistakes: Adopting CQRS by default, before a single model has actually become a proven bottleneck — it's real complexity that should be earned, not assumed.
Underestimating eventual consistency — a write may not be immediately visible in the read model, which can surprise users and callers who don't expect a delay.
Not keeping the read model reliably synchronized with the write model, letting them silently drift out of consistency over time.
Confusing CQRS with simply 'having separate read and write database replicas' — CQRS is about separate MODELS, which is a deeper architectural split than replication alone.
explanation.realWorldExample: Event-sourced systems that maintain separate read projections, e-commerce platforms with a strict order-processing write path and a fast, denormalized product-catalog read path, and analytics dashboards backed by materialized views are all CQRS in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this just having a read replica of the database?

conversation.speaker: The Splitter
conversation.message: A read replica copies the SAME model, just for scaling reads. I go further — the read side can use a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT model, shaped purely for how it's queried, not how it's written.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's the real cost of splitting like this?

conversation.speaker: The Splitter
conversation.message: Eventual consistency. A write might not show up in the read model instantly. That's a genuine trade-off your users and your team both need to understand and design around — not a hidden gotcha to discover in production.

codeBattle.scenario: Your inventory system's write path needs strict, transactional stock validation on every update, while your analytics dashboard needs to run complex aggregate queries across millions of records without slowing down or locking the write path.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Splitter separates strict, transactional writes from fast, denormalized analytics reads, so neither path has to compromise for the other.

quiz.question: What does CQRS separate?
options: The write model (commands) from the read model (queries)
quiz.answer: The write model (commands) from the read model (queries)
quiz.explanation: That's exactly what the name spells out: Command Query Responsibility Segregation.

quiz.question: What's the main trade-off CQRS introduces?
options: Eventual consistency — a write may not be immediately reflected in the read model
It removes the need for a database entirely
It requires the read and write models to be identical
quiz.answer: Eventual consistency — a write may not be immediately reflected in the read model
quiz.explanation: Keeping two separate models in sync typically happens asynchronously, introducing a delay that must be designed around.

quiz.question: How does CQRS differ from simply using a database read replica?
options: CQRS can use a completely different, independently shaped model for reads, not just a copy of the write model
They are identical techniques with different names
Read replicas require CQRS to function
CQRS forbids using a database at all
quiz.answer: CQRS can use a completely different, independently shaped model for reads, not just a copy of the write model
quiz.explanation: A replica copies the same schema for scaling; CQRS's read model can be structured entirely differently, optimized purely for queries.

quiz.question: When should CQRS be avoided?
options: When read and write patterns are similar enough that one model already serves both well
When a single model has become a proven scaling bottleneck
When read and write workloads have very different performance needs
When the team already uses event-driven architecture
quiz.answer: When read and write patterns are similar enough that one model already serves both well
quiz.explanation: CQRS is a scaling pattern that should be earned by a real bottleneck, not adopted by default.
